extracted.intended_audience: Members and committees of Congress, congressional staff, policymakers, and stakeholders interested in U.S. patent law and AI
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes U.S. legal standards and USPTO guidance on (1) whether inventions made using AI can be patented (inventorship) and (2) whether inventions about AI (AI technologies) are patentable (subject-matter eligibility). Focused on federal statutes, case law, and USPTO examiner guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventorship requires conception (mental formation of complete idea)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventorship requires 'conception,' or mentally forming a complete idea for a particular new invention that skilled persons in the relevant field would be able to put into practice without excessive experimentation. A person need not successfully reduce to practice to be an inventor—although conception and reduction to practice may sometimes occur simultaneously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conception is the operative test for whether an individual is an inventor; courts apply the conception standard (not mere assistance or later reduction-to-practice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint inventorship — Pannu factors
rubrics_metrics.description: To qualify as a joint inventor, a person must (1) contribute in a 'significant manner' to the invention, (2) contribute in a way that is not 'insignificant in quality' compared with the whole invention, and (3) contribute more than an explanation of 'well-known concepts and/or the current state of the art.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Joint inventors generally must apply jointly and make required oaths. The Patent Act provides joint inventors need not 'work together or at the same time,' need not make the 'same type or amount of contribution,' and need not contribute to every claim of the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor must be a natural person (Thaler v. Vidal)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Act requires an inventor to be a natural person; an AI system may not be listed as the inventor on a patent. The Federal Circuit held that 'inventor' is an 'individual,' which normally refers to a human being, and policy concerns cannot override statutory text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because Thaler is Federal Circuit precedent and the Supreme Court declined review in that matter, the rule that only humans may be inventors is settled federal law (subject to any future changes by the Supreme Court or Congress).

rubrics_metrics.name: 2024 USPTO Inventorship Guidance — 'significantly contributed' standard for AI-assisted inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2024 Inventorship Guidance stated AI-assisted inventions could be patented so long as at least one natural person 'significantly contributed' to the claimed invention. It explained this is satisfied if at least one human met all three Pannu elements (significant contribution to conception; not insignificant in comparison with the full invention; more than explaining well-known concepts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Human contributions pertaining only to reduction to practice were not sufficient for inventorship. For patents with multiple claims, the 2024 Guidance required a human being to make a significant contribution to each claim. The guidance also acknowledged tools (including AI) 'may perform acts that, if performed by a human, could constitute inventorship under our laws.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 2024 guidance on human-AI contributions — prompting/designing/training vs general goals
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2024 Inventorship Guidance stated that 'prompting, designing, building, or training an AI system "in view of a specific problem to elicit a particular solution"' might constitute a significant contribution, whereas presenting an AI system with only a 'general goal or research plan' would not constitute inventorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing whether a human's interaction with AI rises to inventorship, examine the specificity and problem-directed nature of the human contribution (specific problem/elicited solution = may qualify; general goal = does not).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction to practice alone insufficient for inventorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Human contributions that pertain only to reduction to practice are not sufficient for inventorship, regardless of whether AI was involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventorship analysis focuses on conception, not mere implementation or testing. Activities that only reduce the idea to practice without contributing to the conception do not establish inventorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2025 USPTO Revised Inventorship Guidance — AI as a tool; ordinary conception standard applies
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2025 Inventorship Guidance rescinded the 2024 approach and treats AI as merely a 'tool that assists' in the inventive process, analogous to 'laboratory equipment, computer software, [or] research databases.' It states ordinary standards for inventorship apply regardless of AI use: one or more human inventors must 'conceive' the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 2025 Guidance rejects treating AI as a potential co-inventor under Pannu because Pannu applies to questions among multiple natural persons; when only one natural person used an AI system, the question is whether that human is an inventor under the traditional conception standard. The human must possess 'a definite and permanent idea of the complete invention, such that only ordinary skill is required to reduce the invention to practice.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent-eligible subject matter — Section 101 and judicial exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 101 allows patents on 'any new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter,' but the Supreme Court has recognized judicial exceptions: 'laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas' are not patent-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating whether an AI-related claim is within Section 101, determine whether it is directed to one of the judicial exceptions (e.g., a mathematical formula, mental process) before proceeding to the Alice/Mayo framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice/Mayo two-step test for patent eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 1: Determine whether the patent claims are 'directed to' an ineligible concept (law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea). Step 2: If so, determine whether the elements of each claim contain an 'inventive concept' that transforms the claim into a patent-eligible application of the ineligible concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim limitations that are conventional, routine, and well understood—such as implementing an abstract idea on a generic computer—cannot supply the inventive concept. The test has narrowed patent-eligibility in areas like software, business methods, diagnostics, and biotechnology.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO 2019/AI Eligibility Guidance — two-prong division of Alice step 1: 'recites' and 'integrates'
rubrics_metrics.description: Under USPTO's framework, step 1 of Alice is divided into two prongs: (1) whether the patent claim 'recites' an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomena; and (2) if so, whether the claim has additional elements that 'integrate' the ineligible concept into a practical application of the judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim is patent-eligible if it either does not recite an ineligible concept or if it 'integrates' that concept into a practical application. The AI Eligibility Guidance gives examples: a claim to an application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) for an artificial neural network is eligible because it is directed to specific hardware components and does not recite an abstract idea; a claim on a general method of using a trained neural network to detect anomalies is ineligible (directed to an abstract mathematical/mental process implemented on generic components).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical application/inventive-concept standard for AI claims — 'improv[ing] the functioning of a computer or ... another technology or technical field'
rubrics_metrics.description: AI inventions may be eligible when they 'integrate' an abstract idea into a practical application by 'improv[ing] the functioning of a computer or improv[ing] another technology or technical field.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a general deep neural network method to analyze speech is ineligible as abstract, but a particular method that separates mixed speech into separate waveforms and recombines them without unwanted sources may be an eligible practical application. Evaluate whether the claim recites technical improvements or specific applications to a technological field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of USPTO guidance and role of courts/Congress
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO guidance documents (e.g., Inventorship Guidance, AI Eligibility Guidance) are intended to guide examiners but do not themselves carry the force of law and are not legally binding on courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties can challenge USPTO decisions in federal court; courts may interpret the Patent Act differently. Congress may amend the Patent Act if it wishes to change or clarify law governing AI-assisted inventions or AI-technology eligibility. Policymakers may monitor how USPTO guidance fares in practice before legislating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical/administrative considerations and stakeholder perspectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Stakeholders differ on how USPTO guidance treats AI: some view the 2025 guidance as providing 'certainty' and consistent with pro-patent policy; others criticize USPTO examples as unrealistic or argue guidance treats trained AI as a 'generic computer' and may make obtaining AI patents unnecessarily difficult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When crafting or evaluating guidance/policy, consider (a) clarity and realistic examples, (b) whether claim limitations tied to AI are treated as generic or technical, and (c) how guidance aligns with or diverges from case law (and potential legislative responses).
